content:
This is the topic for discussions on the Tau Ceti roadmap of Representation Theory/SpinRepresentations.

Starting this topic because I'm currently pouring my subscription quota and personal attention bandwidth into this roadmap (particularly on Clifford Algebras and Spin groups), and would like to discuss on Zulip.

For this roadmap, 15 PRs merged so far, 7 mine (of fluctuating quality). I have mixed feelings towards formalization by agents in familiar math areas, particularly unclear whether agent work could eventually qualify for upstreaming to mathlib, but the only way to learn something in the process is to actively participate.

Besides polishing my harness/infra (e.g. skills in addition to Tau Ceti rubrics and coordination) to work on this, I also revisit PR review churn, reusable bits, and routes through the roadmap. The goal is to improve PR quality, turn reusable bits into refactor PRs and roadmap adjustments, and reach milestones via routes in parallel.

So for discussions on the roadmap, I would like to share a visualized and annotated map of my routes through the roadmap (currently 4 personal goals each with its summit, mostly independent, sharing a few stretches) which I use locally for selecting next slice of work to PR (accompanied by PR-annotated roadmap). The routes may not make sense in math or optimized for reuse due to trying to stay independent.

There are certainly sloppy bits that slipped through, but glossing over them quickly should capture the human intent.

For my routes through the roadmap , I extended each goal so their summits make more sense in math, also updated PR status.

I'm not claiming these routes, it is just an expression of intent, and an observation on interesting routes. My agents would steer clear of other PRs.

Utensil Song said:

For this roadmap, 15 PRs merged so far, 7 mine (of fluctuating quality).

I'm confused by this statement, I see 289 PRs merged with the roadmap/RepresentationTheory label.

And, um, I'm a bit worried, @Utensil Song. Do you have any evidence your skills are helping? I have reasonably strong evidence that they are hurting: asking an agent to rank 10 PRs, 5 of yours and 5 others, randomly selected from the RepresentationTheory roadmap, but not telling it who they were authored by, it put all of yours below all of the others.

In particular, in summary it said:

the bottom five are more often assembly and transport of results proved in earlier PRs, diluted by duplicated helpers and definition-restating lemmas.

Could I suggest that you either remove your custom instructions, or put some effort into obtaining evidence about the efficacy of your custom instructions?

Kim Morrison said:

I see 289 PRs merged with the roadmap/RepresentationTheory label.

Sorry for the confusion, this topic was intended to discuss Roadmap: RepresentationTheory/SpinRepresentations (as the content showed), but copying the label during drafting the opening message, caused the oversight. I have fixed the title and wording in place.

all of yours below all of the others

I failed to reproduce the same ranking result (given only rank them by TauCeti rubrics and nothing more) with GPT-5.6 Sol with both high and xhigh effort. Since now I have 10 merged PRs, I mixed them with 10 other (randomly sampled once then fixed) PRs from the whole RepresentationTheory. Here is one of such clean conversation on ChatGPT Work to rule out the influence from any local agent instructions: https://chatgpt.com/share/6a78666f-debc-83eb-874f-7a24d5e645d4

There is no clear sign of consistently poor quality or higher PR friction. Time trend analysis shows quality drop on Aug 3-4 when I struggled with next work selection on the roadmap hence the effort on figuring out better routes.

Near the end of the conversation, Sol says:

  1. assembly and transport of results proved in earlier PRs is due to intentional consequences of the roadmap and sample selectionwhich is consistent with my impression and how I picked these initial PRs to control scale and complexity.
  2. diluted by duplicated helpers and definition-restating lemmas is due to

    The roadmap decomposed one construction into many tightly coupled PRs, but generation remained PR-local and implementation began before the shared canonical API was designed and stabilized.

Particularly, "Each downstream PR became the first real API test of its predecessor." I think it partially reflects my failure to have a clear route before asking agents to select the next slice of work based on local eval of previous PR, and partially reflects some API needs are discovered by the consumer's golf and abstraction during review. I have to admit that if I had chosen simply sweep from lower layers would have less such churn.

Do you have any evidence your skills are helping?

They might inherit something bad from my personal formalization attempts, but are mostly learned during these PRs. My original perception is that with only current rubrics and coordination, my agents with Sol /Terra high+ (I tweaked the combinations across PRs) can't deliver stably, especially some PRs kept getting contradicted change requests from different review agents and ending with contest. These are the intial motivations to distill these skills, the recon, design, golf ones are particularly there to help discovering such issues before opening the PR or hitting local review.

put some effort into obtaining evidence about the efficacy of your custom instructions

Initially I shared the skills in the sense of "polishing in public", not claiming that they are good. I will do more ablation experiments against local rubric reviews, as I do know that skills might hurt the performance of frontier models.

Thank you for the observations and I will further root-cause and address them. I am also auditing all recently merged PRs to identify process and quality issues, and will rework open PRs with stricter local review.

One more thing I noticed is that I used draft PR to stack on open PRs under review, they had recieved additional Claude review comment warning about 2 PRs having identical changes (and the normal refactor breaking warning).

If stacking draft PRs are not encouraged practice, I will stop them (currently I observed no waste of review rounds, but draft PRs would still trigger CI).

Thanks for the responses. I will take another look when I get time.

Yes, I think it's best to avoid stacked PRs. The Tau Ceti review process won't cope.

Thanks for your patience. After agent audit and manual review, it is confirmed that PR quality and review churn fluctuate, 3 PRs ranked at bottom are closed manually.

I have applied the following measures, aiming to stably stay above the median of sampled PRs, particularly with review churn:

  1. Hardened 2+1 review: before opening PR, local work must pass dual review by both pure Tau Ceti rubrics and my review skills, then an additional round review of pure Tau Ceti rubrics to simulate as if already opened and reviewed externally, and this will be removed after dual review quality stablizes;
  2. Review skills simplied and flatterned: one earlier effort refactored the review skill as extensions of Tau Ceti rubrics and have restated Tau Ceti rubrics as summary at the extension point, I personally suspect this is hurting full compliance to pure Tau Ceti rubrics, and have flattern extensions as only few additional skill rubrics to cope with issues frequently found by external reviews.

All draft PRs are being reworked with these measures, possibly rescoped (local design, reuse, and generality findings now may trigger rescope of the PR), no further stacked draft PRs will be created.

I have also added a footer to PR bodies to be transparent about models used and local review efforts prior to PR open, e.g.:

:robot: GPT-5.6 Sol high · rubrics @ b8161ef · local 2+1 review @ 94d88d5 fixed: documentation (1), reuse (1)

Recent open and merged PRs have been backfilled with this footer.

Thanks, @Utensil Song. I've taken a look too at those PRs, and I agree they were okay!

Nice to see people experimenting with the agent setups being used to contribute to Tau Ceti. It is a big landscape to explore.

(And a more general note: even if someone comes up with an agent setup that is demonstrably worse than the defaults, it is critical that Tau Ceti can cope with this, through review and refactoring! It's part of making this a robust system.)

Completed 1 of 4 goals on the route map, and PR health (quality and churn) seems to have stablized, but we still have some serious outliners, which were caught by my PR health monitor and closed to reassess and rework as a whole (was 3 hours but now shorten to 1 hours).

Below the routes of the roadmap, I set up model-free monitors on PR activities and health, and audited from different angles, including Kim's 10+ refactor PRs on my feat PRs, improvements were deployed.

My deep audit has found the root causes of the fluctuating PR health (last 2 days I have applied more improvements yet resulted in more outliners so we can learn the common factors through lens of later replacement efforts). Full but concise audit report is attached for agent consumption and I have read them in full, and addressed them with focused remediations.

During the audit I asked many questions but here is a one-liner: Is any of stale mathlib pin, challenging math/formalization, missing roadmap bridges, missing rubric rules, local review compliance, skill defects, not using TauCetiWorker causing the health issues?

The opening section of the audit report has the conclusion summary, here is my perception (1&2 are the root cause, 4 amplifies, 3 is nice to fix):

  1. Agent setup: I mistook the TauCetiWorker as a tool for reviewers, and agent treated it as optional and developed its own mechansims to inherit prior experience, handle feedbacks and steering during the process, but not even checked its reference design; collectively we missed it together, and missing its review engine design is fatal to 2;
  2. Reviewer gate: I thought frontier models have advanced agentic behavior, so I used raw codex (unlike I used OMC for Claude Code) but it assigned review subagents that suffered context contaminations and rubric distraction, so not equivalent to external review agents, 2+1 is extra effort locally but didn't address the root cause of not using cleanroom, per-rubric subagents;
  3. Author design: Consistent lack of 3 design considerations at author phase, exposed design flaws when formalizing harder part of the math; they are not hurt by skills, and they can be remediated by recon/design skills, and such skill may not emerge by just pointing Sol High at it (higher reasoning level may discover them but would not be proportional, I intend to use them in later refactors);
  4. Difficulty amplifier: Formalizing the harder part of math exposed the design flaws, especially when agents needed to design reusable intermediate Lean APIs where roadmap didn't specify them or had just stubs that couldn't help bridging.

Kind of expected this to happen at some point: two roadmap small edit PRs are opened and ready for review.

TauCetiRoadmap#224 unblocks TauCeti#3078, the original wording is harmless for humans, a human might easily infer the intended split, but reviewer agents took it literally and requested a roadmap clarification, so we need to split the deps explicitly. I have examined the changes and math, see https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/pull/224#issuecomment-5300730872 .

TauCetiRoadmap#225 unblocks the next three algebraic Bott slices after it to achieve goal alpha on my route map (currently I have three of them ready locally, waiting for the roadmap review). The dependency branching is partially demonstrated by earlier merged lean PRs, and the roadmap before revision is expected to block future lean reviews. See also https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCetiRoadmap/pull/225#issuecomment-5300794746 for math discussion.
